## Overview

How quickly does a pest–natural-enemy system return after it is disturbed, and how does
temperature change that? This tutorial measures resilience in three ways, each suited to a
different kind of PBDM:

1. **An equilibrium** of the consumer–resource theory model [@WangGutierrez1980Stability]: the
   return rate of its linearisation, followed along temperature until stability is lost.
2. **An annual cycle** of a daily-step host–parasitoid model under weather that repeats every
   year: the cycle's Floquet multipliers [@Klausmeier2008Floquet], the eigenvalues of the map that
   takes the state on 1 January to the state a year later.
3. **A trajectory under real weather**, which has neither an equilibrium nor a cycle: recovery
   after a spray, from paired simulations that share the same weather.

The metrics come from [ResilienceCore.jl](https://github.com/ecorecipes/ResilienceCore.jl) and
[DynamicalResilience.jl](https://github.com/ecorecipes/DynamicalResilience.jl). This package
supplies the PBDM side: `linearise` for theory equilibria, `consumer_resource_problem`, an
integrator for `PBDMProblem` (`init`, `step!`, `reinit!`, `set_u!`), `full_state`,
`annual_map` and `annual_fixed_point`.

## Setup

```{julia}
using PhysiologicallyBasedDemographicModels
using DynamicalResilience
using CairoMakie
using LinearAlgebra
using Printf
using Downloads
```

## 1. Resilience against temperature: the consumer–resource equilibrium

The theory helpers find the interior equilibrium of a resource (logistic, rate `r`, capacity
`K`) and a consumer with a Fraser–Gilbert functional response whose respiration rises with
temperature (Q₁₀). `linearise` turns the result into ResilienceCore's `ContinuousJacobian`, so
the resilience metrics apply directly.

```{julia}
fr = FraserGilbertResponse(0.8)
resp = Q10Respiration(0.02, 2.0, 25.0)
cr = (intrinsic_rate = 1.0, carrying_capacity = 1000.0, consumer_demand_rate = 0.5,
      conversion_efficiency = 0.4)

eq = find_equilibrium(fr, resp, 25.0; cr...)
J = linearise(eq)
@printf("At 25 °C: M₁* = %.1f, M₂* = %.1f (%s)\n", eq.M1_star, eq.M2_star, eq.classification)
@printf("  resilience = %.4f per day, reactivity = %.4f per day\n", resilience(J), reactivity(J))
```

To follow the equilibrium along temperature, the same model is available as an `ODEProblem`
whose parameters include `T`. DynamicalResilience's `resilience_along` re-solves the
equilibrium at each temperature (warm-starting from the last), linearises it, and reports where
stability is lost and how: a **fold** when a real eigenvalue reaches zero, a **Hopf** when a
complex pair crosses the imaginary axis.

```{julia}
prob_cr = consumer_resource_problem(fr, resp, 0.0; cr...)
temperatures = 0.0:0.25:60.0
along = resilience_along(prob_cr, (p, T) -> merge(p, (T = T,)), temperatures; u0 = prob_cr.u0)
println("transition: ", along.transition)
```

```{julia}
#| label: fig-cr-temperature
#| fig-cap: "Return rate (resilience) and reactivity of the consumer–resource equilibrium against temperature. Shading marks where the equilibrium was found but is unstable."
fig1 = Figure(size = (820, 360))
ax1 = Axis(fig1[1, 1], xlabel = "Temperature (°C)", ylabel = "per day", title = "(a) Return rate and reactivity")
ok = along.converged
lines!(ax1, temperatures[ok], along.metrics.resilience[ok], label = "resilience", linewidth = 2.5)
lines!(ax1, temperatures[ok], along.metrics.reactivity[ok], label = "reactivity", linewidth = 2.5, linestyle = :dash)
hlines!(ax1, [0.0], color = :gray, linewidth = 1)
axislegend(ax1, position = :rt)
ax2 = Axis(fig1[1, 2], xlabel = "Temperature (°C)", ylabel = "biomass", title = "(b) Equilibrium")
lines!(ax2, temperatures[ok], [u[1] for u in along.equilibrium[ok]], label = "resource M₁*", linewidth = 2.5)
lines!(ax2, temperatures[ok], [u[2] for u in along.equilibrium[ok]], label = "consumer M₂*", linewidth = 2.5)
axislegend(ax2, position = :rt)
fig1
```

## 2. Annual cycles: oleander scale and *Aphytis chilensis*

For a daily-step model driven by seasonal weather the natural object is the **annual map**
`F`: the state on day 1 sent to the state a year later, with the same weather year each time.
Its fixed point is the model's annual cycle, and the eigenvalues of its Jacobian there are the
cycle's Floquet multipliers. A cycle is stable when every multiplier has modulus below one, and
the leading modulus ρ is the factor by which a small disturbance shrinks per year; the
resilience is `−log ρ` per year.

The model is the single-parasitoid scenario of the oleander scale vignette
[@Gutierrez2007OleanderScale]: scale with temperature-dependent fecundity and logistic crowding
up to a cap of 500, and *A. chilensis* attacking it with a ratio-dependent response, both above
their thermal thresholds. It is small (two state variables) and density-dependent, so its annual
cycles are quick to find. As it turns out, the analysis is most useful here as a diagnosis of
the model itself.

```{julia}
const SCALE_TL = 10.0
const SCALE_MU_NYMPH = 0.001
const AC_TL, AC_SEARCH, AC_DD_IMMATURE = 11.0, 0.15, 200.0

function scale_fecundity(T)
    (T < 12.0 || T > 34.0) && return 0.0
    return 4.0 * max(0.0, 1 - ((T - 23.0) / 11.0)^2)
end

function scale_problem(weather; tspan = (1, 365), scale0 = 50.0, par0 = 1.0)
    scale_bp = BulkPopulation(:scale, scale0; K = 500.0, growth_fn = (N, w, day, p) -> begin
        T = w.T_mean
        N + N * scale_fecundity(T) * 0.1 * (1 - N / 500) - SCALE_MU_NYMPH * max(0.0, T - SCALE_TL) * N
    end)
    par_bp = BulkPopulation(:parasitoid, par0)
    parasitism = CustomRule(:parasitism, (sys, w, day, p) -> begin
        dd_par = max(0.0, w.T_mean - p.par_TL)
        S = total_population(sys[:scale].population)
        P = total_population(sys[:parasitoid].population)
        attacked = 0.0
        if dd_par > 0 && P > 0
            attacked = min(p.par_search * (1 - exp(-0.5 * S / max(P, 0.1))) * P, 0.5 * S)
            remove_fraction!(sys, :scale, clamp(attacked / max(S, 1e-10), 0.0, 1.0))
            sys[:parasitoid].population.value[] =
                max(0.0, P + attacked * 0.3 * dd_par / p.par_dd_immature - 0.003 * dd_par * P)
        else
            sys[:parasitoid].population.value[] = max(0.0, P * 0.999)
        end
        return (attacked = attacked,)
    end)
    system = PopulationSystem(:scale => scale_bp, :parasitoid => par_bp)
    return PBDMProblem(MultiSpeciesPBDMNew(), system, weather, tspan;
        p = (par_TL = AC_TL, par_search = AC_SEARCH, par_dd_immature = AC_DD_IMMATURE),
        rules = AbstractInteractionRule[parasitism])
end
```

The coastal climate of vignette 32 is a sinusoid with mean 14.5 °C and amplitude 3.5 °C
peaking in mid-July; `SinusoidalWeather` with `phase = 191.25` reproduces it. We find the
annual cycle there (30 plain years first, then Newton's method on the annual map) and read off
its multipliers.

```{julia}
coastal = SinusoidalWeather(14.5, 3.5; phase = 191.25)
prob_coast = scale_problem(coastal)
cycle = annual_fixed_point(prob_coast; spinup = 30)
@printf("annual cycle on 1 January: scale = %.2f, parasitoid = %.3f (converged: %s)\n",
        cycle.u[1], cycle.u[2], cycle.converged)
println("Floquet multipliers: ", round.(cycle.multipliers; digits = 4))
@printf("leading modulus ρ = %.4f, resilience = %.4f per year\n",
        maximum(abs, cycle.multipliers), resilience(cycle.jacobian))
```

The cycle has **no parasitoid**: starting from one *A. chilensis*, the parasitoid dies out, and
the annual cycle is the scale's alone. With the parasitoid absent, the Jacobian is triangular
(next year's parasitoids do not depend on this year's scale when there are none), so its two
diagonal entries are the two multipliers:

- the **scale's**, which measures how fast the scale's own annual cycle forgets a disturbance;
- the **parasitoid's**, its growth factor per year when rare. Below one, *A. chilensis* cannot
  invade the scale's cycle; above one, it can.

`annual_fixed_point` differentiates an absent species from above (populations are clipped at
zero, so the map has a kink there): a central difference across the kink would halve the
parasitoid's multiplier.

Now the same calculation as the whole year warms or cools: the mean temperature shifts with the
seasonal shape held fixed.

```{julia}
means = 10.0:0.5:24.0
m_scale = fill(NaN, length(means))
m_par = fill(NaN, length(means))
scale_jan = fill(NaN, length(means))
par_jan = fill(NaN, length(means))
for (k, Tm) in enumerate(means)
    prob = scale_problem(SinusoidalWeather(Tm, 3.5; phase = 191.25))
    fp = annual_fixed_point(prob; spinup = 30)
    fp.converged || continue
    scale_jan[k], par_jan[k] = fp.u
    J = fp.jacobian.J
    m_scale[k], m_par[k] = J[1, 1], J[2, 2]
end
println("parasitoid absent on every cycle: ", all(x -> abs(x) < 1e-10, par_jan))
for k in 1:4:length(means)
    @printf("mean %4.1f °C: scale on 1 Jan = %6.1f, scale multiplier = %.2e, parasitoid invasion factor = %.2e\n",
            means[k], scale_jan[k], m_scale[k], m_par[k])
end
```

```{julia}
#| label: fig-floquet
#| fig-cap: "Floquet multipliers of the oleander scale's annual cycle against mean temperature. The parasitoid's multiplier is its growth factor per year when rare: below 1 everywhere, so *Aphytis chilensis* cannot invade. The scale's multiplier is how much of a disturbance to the scale survives a year."
fig2 = Figure(size = (820, 360))
ax3 = Axis(fig2[1, 1], xlabel = "Mean annual temperature (°C)", ylabel = "multiplier per year", yscale = log10,
           title = "(a) Floquet multipliers")
lines!(ax3, means, max.(m_par, 1e-12), label = "A. chilensis (invasion)", linewidth = 2.5)
lines!(ax3, means, max.(m_scale, 1e-12), label = "scale", linewidth = 2.5, linestyle = :dash)
hlines!(ax3, [1.0], color = :gray, linestyle = :dot)
axislegend(ax3, position = :rt)
ax4 = Axis(fig2[1, 2], xlabel = "Mean annual temperature (°C)", ylabel = "scale on 1 January",
           title = "(b) The scale's annual cycle")
lines!(ax4, means, scale_jan, linewidth = 2.5)
fig2
```

## 3. Recovery after a spray under real weather

Real weather is not periodic, so there is no cycle to linearise. Instead we ask how long the
system takes to forget a disturbance along the trajectory the weather actually produces. The
integrator lets DynamicalResilience's `recovery` run two simulations of the same years: a
control, and a replay (`reinit!`) in which a spray removes half the scale on a given day. The
distance between them, over the following days, is the system's memory of the spray.

The weather is a daily AgMERRA reanalysis series [@Ruane2015AgMERRA] for a Mediterranean grid
point (35.9° N, 0.1° E), the sample bundled with the Free Pascal port of the CASAS cassava
model. It is used here only as a realistic, irregular weather record for a Mediterranean
climate, not as a site where this scale–parasitoid pair has been studied.

```{julia}
wx_url = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ecorecipes/pascal-pbdm-cassava-fpc/" *
         "296d825f761ef104afe1a80ccd5c0ef9aae01613/cassava/wx.det.txt"
lines_wx = readlines(Downloads.download(wx_url))
rows = [split(l) for l in lines_wx[4:end] if !isempty(strip(l))]
years = [parse(Int, r[3]) for r in rows]
tmax = [parse(Float64, r[4]) for r in rows]
tmin = [parse(Float64, r[5]) for r in rows]
keep = (years .== 1985) .| (years .== 1986)
days_wx = [DailyWeather((a + b) / 2, b, a) for (a, b) in zip(tmax[keep], tmin[keep])]
real_weather = WeatherSeries(days_wx)
@printf("%d days of 1985–86; daily mean %.1f–%.1f °C\n", length(days_wx),
        minimum(d.T_mean for d in days_wx), maximum(d.T_mean for d in days_wx))
```

We start the run from the coastal annual cycle found above, so the parasitoid is absent and this
is the scale's own recovery, and spray on day 120 (late April) or day 240 (late August).

```{julia}
prob_real = scale_problem(real_weather; tspan = (1, length(days_wx)), scale0 = cycle.u[1], par0 = cycle.u[2])
spray(u, rng) = (v = copy(u); v[1] *= 0.5; v)
scale_only(u) = u[1:1]
runs = Dict(day => recovery(prob_real, DirectIteration(); perturb = spray, observe = scale_only,
                            t_pulse = day, horizon = 300, interval = 1, tol = 0.05)
            for day in (120, 240))
for day in (120, 240)
    r = runs[day]
    @printf("spray on day %d: scale removed %.2f; back within 5%% after %s days; return rate %.4f per day\n",
            day, r.distance[1], r.return_time, r.return_rate)
end
```

```{julia}
#| label: fig-recovery
#| fig-cap: "Distance in scale density between sprayed and unsprayed runs under 1985–86 AgMERRA weather, relative to the amount removed, for a spray on day 120 or day 240."
fig3 = Figure(size = (820, 360))
ax5 = Axis(fig3[1, 1], xlabel = "Days since spray", ylabel = "relative distance", yscale = log10,
           title = "Recovery after removing half the scale")
for day in (120, 240)
    r = runs[day]
    lines!(ax5, r.t, max.(r.distance ./ r.distance[1], 1e-8), label = "day $day", linewidth = 2.5)
end
hlines!(ax5, [0.05], color = :gray, linestyle = :dash)
axislegend(ax5, position = :rt)
fig3
```

## Reading the results

**The consumer–resource equilibrium recovers faster as it warms, until it fails.** At 25 °C it
is a stable node with a return rate of 0.023 per day (a disturbance shrinks by a factor of *e*
in about 43 days) and reactivity 0.059 per day: some disturbances grow at first
[@NeubertCaswell1997Transients]. Warming raises the consumer's respiration, so its equilibrium
falls and the resource's rises; the return rate climbs to about 0.17 per day near 50 °C, the
return becomes oscillatory (a stable focus) between about 45 and 52 °C, and reactivity turns
negative above about 40 °C. Stability is lost near 58 °C. `resilience_along` labels this a
fold because a real eigenvalue reaches zero, but it is a transcritical point: the consumer's
equilibrium meets zero as its metabolic compensation point reaches one, rather than meeting a
saddle and disappearing. The label distinguishes real from complex crossings only.

**In the oleander scale model the parasitoid cannot invade, at any temperature.** Every annual
cycle has the scale alone. The parasitoid's multiplier, its growth factor per year when rare,
is 0.41 at a mean of 10 °C and falls steadily with warming, to about 0.04 at 14 °C and 10⁻⁶ at
24 °C: warmer years carry more degree-days of parasitoid loss. This explains why vignette 32
finds the same scale density with *A. chilensis*, with *C. utilis*, or with both: in that
model's parasitoid equation the gain per degree-day (at most 0.15 × 0.3 / 200 ≈ 0.0002 per
parasitoid) is about thirteen times smaller than the loss (0.003), so the parasitoids always
decline. The annual-cycle analysis finds this in seconds, where simulations of a few years only
show the parasitoids drifting down.

**The scale's own multiplier is an artefact of its cap.** It is 6 × 10⁻⁴ at 10 °C and exactly
zero from 12 °C up, because on those cycles the scale reaches the carrying-capacity cap of 500
in summer, and `BulkPopulation` clips it there: any disturbance is erased once the cap is
reached. Under real weather the same thing shows up as fast recovery: removing half the scale in
late April or late August is undone to within 5% in 11–12 days, at a return rate of about 0.4
per day, as logistic growth refills the cap.

## Caveats

- **Linearisation is local.** Return rates and multipliers describe small disturbances near an
  equilibrium or cycle; a spray that removes half the scale is not small, which is why the
  recovery runs are simulated rather than linearised.
- **The annual map repeats one weather year.** Its fixed point is the cycle under that year
  forever; under real, varying weather the system never settles onto it.
- **Finite differences.** The annual map's Jacobian is taken by central finite differences,
  because PBDM states are stored as `Float64` and do not carry dual numbers.
- **Model scope.** The scale–parasitoid model is the simplified single-parasitoid scenario of
  vignette 32, and the real weather is a sample record, not a site-specific study.
